Offline RL

Offline RL learns from a fixed log of experience, collected earlier by some other policy, with no chance to try anything new. It matters wherever exploring is costly or dangerous: medicine, driving, robots. The trap is that Q-learning's max happily picks actions that never appear in the log, whose values were never corrected.

The log: a careful driver crossed Lesson 53's cliff by the second row, taking a random action with probability $\varepsilon$. You choose how much data there is and how random it was. Then two learners train on the same log, offline.

visits in the log cliff arrow: greedy action red arrow: action never in the log

Both learners iterate the Q-learning backup over the whole log until it stops changing ($\gamma = 0.95$, values start at 0). The real run lasts at most 50 steps and its return is undiscounted. Try $\varepsilon = 0$ first.

The maths

The log is a fixed dataset $\mathcal D$ of transitions $(s, a, r, s')$ from a behaviour policy $\beta$. Offline Q-learning repeatedly applies, averaging over the logged transitions from $(s, a)$:

$$Q(s, a) \leftarrow \operatorname*{mean}_{\mathcal D} \Big[ r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') \Big]$$

Only pairs that appear in $\mathcal D$ are ever updated. Every other $Q(s', a')$ keeps its initial value, here 0. The rewards are all negative, so every action the log has tried looks worse than every action it has not. The max picks the unknown, and the greedy policy walks into territory, or a cliff, that no data describes.

This is distribution shift. The values are accurate only where the data distribution $d^\beta(s, a)$ has mass. The learned policy $\pi$ visits different states and actions, $d^\pi \ne d^\beta$, exactly where the values are fiction. Online, the agent would try those actions, be disappointed and correct them (Lesson 8). Offline it never can.

The fix is to stay where the data is. Batch-constrained Q-learning (Fujimoto et al., 2019) restricts the max and the policy to actions seen in the log:

$$Q(s, a) \leftarrow \operatorname*{mean}_{\mathcal D} \Big[ r + \gamma \max_{a' : (s', a') \in \mathcal D} Q(s', a') \Big]$$

It can still beat the behaviour policy, by stitching together the best pieces of different logged episodes. Conservative Q-learning (Kumar et al., 2020) does the same job with function approximation: it adds a penalty that pushes down the values of all actions and pushes up those in the data,

$$\alpha\, \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathcal D}\Big[ \log \sum_a e^{Q(s, a)} - \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \beta(\cdot \mid s)} Q(s, a) \Big]$$

so actions the data never tried end up looking worse, not better.
